d.title: A hundred and thirty times faster, and only if it is sorted
d.caption: **Setting the index is not what makes the lookup fast — sorting it is.** An unsorted index still scans, at the same 4 ms as filtering on a column, and nothing in the code looks different. `is_monotonic_increasing` is the one-line check worth running before you believe a lookup is cheap. **The cost side is real too: a meaningful index changes how half of pandas behaves**, turns a routine column operation into a reset-and-set, and most output formats ignore it. Set one when you look rows up by that key repeatedly, join on it, or need time slicing — not by reflex.

d.title: The blank label is display only, and that misleads everybody once
d.caption: **pandas suppresses a repeated outer label for readability, so the second row appears to have no region — and the label is there, as `g.index[1]` shows.** Every tuple is complete. You will meet a MultiIndex whether or not you want one, because any groupby on two columns returns one. **Two things make it workable: sort the levels, because slicing an inner level requires lexsorted levels**, and use IndexSlice rather than guessing at nested brackets. When none of that is wanted, `reset_index` turns the levels back into ordinary columns.

d.title: The same 500,000 strings, three ways, and the default is the worst
d.caption: **Eleven times the memory and fifteen times the time, for the dtype you get if you do nothing** — `object` holds pointers to Python strings, so every `.str` call is a Python loop. The Arrow-backed string dtype stores contiguous bytes with offsets and runs in C. **Categorical wins on both counts here only because there are four distinct values**, and it would lose on high-cardinality text. The quiet benefit of the last two rows is the missing-value behaviour: `object` can hold `None` *or* `NaN` inconsistently, while the string dtype uses `pd.NA` every time.

d.title: Five ways to deal with a hole, and the first one is almost never right
d.caption: **`dropna()` with no arguments removes a row if *any* column is missing, which on a wide frame can delete nearly everything** — here six rows become one. The arguments are where the control is: `subset` for the columns you actually care about, `thresh` for a tolerance, `axis=1` to drop sparse columns instead of rows. **And the habit worth adopting before any of it: add the indicator column first.** Whether a value was missing is frequently more predictive than whatever you fill in, and filling erases it — one extra column preserves the signal and makes the imputation choice far less critical.

d.title: Two primitives, and everything else is a convenience over them
d.caption: **`stack` and `unstack` move a level between the axes, and that is all any reshape does** — `pivot` is unstack after set_index, and `melt` is stack after set_index plus reset_index. Knowing that pair means never having to remember which function goes which way. **`unstack` on a grouped result is the single most useful application:** a groupby on two columns gives a MultiIndexed Series, and one call turns it into the cross-tab people actually wanted. The two to watch are in the last rows: `explode` duplicates the index, and `pivot_table` averages by default.

d.title: Three scores tied, and five different ways to rank them
d.caption: **The default averages the tied positions, so three people tied for second all get rank 3 and nobody is second or fourth** — statistically defensible, and odd on a leaderboard. `min` is the competition ranking most people mean: 1, 2, 2, 2, 5. `first` breaks ties by position in the data, which is arbitrary but stable. **The choice is a presentation decision, and the default is rarely the one you would choose if asked**, which is why it is worth passing `method` explicitly every time rather than discovering the fractional ranks in a report.
